notes: \cpara{Opens with an old joke. Diogenes Laertius reports that when Plato defined man as ``an animal, biped and featherless,'' Diogenes plucked a fowl and brought it in, saying ``Here is Plato's man.'' In the story the definition was then patched: ``there was added to the definition, `having broad nails.''' That is the kind of definition the previous post describes, a list of features for recognizing members.}
\cpara{Describes the usual form of an argument by definition, with ``usually'': visible features, a dictionary, a conclusion. The atheism conclusion is introduced here and taken up near the end.}

\cpara{Argues that a premise both sides accept cannot be what the dispute is about: if the listener doubted Socrates's two legs, the premise would be useless. The inference is hedged (``probably'') and it is sound.}
\cpara{Grants the legitimate move from visible to hidden properties, and grounds it in clusters of similar things in the world, not in definitions or common usage.}
\cpara{Adds that no definition changes the clusters. The definition ``all featherless bipeds except Socrates'' is a joke that makes the point.}
\cpara{Models the correct form: observed features, then a guess (``I'm going to guess''), then a prediction. The inference is stated as probable, as the post says it should be.}
\cpara{Adds a new piece of evidence that bears directly on the prediction: an antidote.}
\cpara{Draws the consequence: once the evidence is specific, the dispute has to move to biochemistry, and the label settles nothing.}

\cpara{Restates the answer for this use of the phrase, with ``usually''.}

\cpara{States the rule in general form, ``on exactly those occasions''. It is a claim about when people use the phrase; the evidence the post offers for it is the author's informal tally in the last two paragraphs.}

\cpara{The second use, ``X, by definition, is a Y!'' The atheism argument is the author's own wording of a common claim; no one is quoted. The post does not say here which connotation of ``religion'' is being sneaked in. ``The Argument from Common Usage'' had named two: that atheism's reasoning methods, or its record of violence, are ``on a par'' with those of religions.}
\cpara{Contrasts a central member of the category, for which no one needs the phrase.}
\cpara{Concludes that the phrase is needed only for a member unlike the category's central cases.}
\cpara{The general conclusion, joining this post to the previous one.}

\clogic{This covers the debater's argument above. It does not cover a definition that is itself a rule assigning consequences, as in law. American courts have classed atheism as a religion for First Amendment purposes, although it does not resemble the central members. In Kaufman v. McCaughtry (7th Cir. 2005) the court wrote: ``Atheism is Kaufman's religion, and the group that he wanted to start was religious in nature even though it expressly rejects a belief in a supreme being.'' The classification applied the court's definition of religion, and the court found that refusing an atheist prisoner's request to form a study group had violated his rights; no connotation was needed. I quote the ruling from the First Amendment Encyclopedia and could not open the opinion itself.}

\cpara{The evidence for the rule: the author's tally over thirteen years, kept ``not with literal statistics,'' as the post says, and read by ``eyeballing''. The other alarm signals listed come without support; the link on ``Hitler'' goes to Godwin's Law.}

\cpara{Admits exceptions, the first by Feynman, without showing any of them, and advises dropping the phrase anyway. The closing joke uses the phrase in the way just warned against; that is the joke.}
